question: A researcher has checked most of a twenty-claim brief but two claims could not be confirmed against any source before her deadline. What should she do with those two?
options: A) Delete them quietly, on the basis that a brief containing only verified claims is the safest thing to circulate.
B) Keep them but mark them clearly as unconfirmed, so readers know which parts rest on nothing she could check.
C) Leave them in the brief unchanged, since they were not shown to be wrong and removing them would weaken it.
D) Soften their wording so they read as more tentative, which lowers the risk without drawing attention to them.
correct_answers: B) Keep them but mark them clearly as unconfirmed, so readers know which parts rest on nothing she could check.
explanations: Silent deletion hides that a question was raised and not resolved, and a later reader may reintroduce the same claim having no idea it was doubted.

Correct. Marking them preserves information the reader needs and shows exactly where the evidence stops, which lets anyone relying on the brief decide whether those two points matter to their decision.
Presented alongside verified claims and in the same voice, unconfirmed claims inherit the credibility of the ones that were checked.
Hedged wording signals mild uncertainty rather than absent verification, and it deliberately avoids making the gap visible.
